← Tuckpointing bid calculator

How much to charge for tuckpointing

Masons get shopped on a published $8 / sq ft tuckpointing Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the joints or the access. A ground-level Type N smear of a ranch veneer is a different job from a three-story historic lime grind with a swing stage, lintels, and cut-and-replace brick.

Open the free tuckpointing bid calculator

Price the joints and the access, not the $8 dump

Tuckpointing is a face, then a method, then how you reach it. Length times height is the wall. Joint lineal feet is that area times a density for the bond. A smear is a surface coat. Grind-and-point is the real trade. Rebuild is cut-out and relay. Ground is a ladder. Two stories is scaffold. Three stories is a swing stage.

A smear is not a grind

The cheap special is almost always a surface coat on a one-story ranch, no grind, Type N bags. Proper tuckpointing grinds the joint out, then points it. Matching a smear per-foot number on a grind-and-scaffold job is how a sold wall becomes a two-day loss after the first scaffold ticket.

Lintels, brick, and lime are not in the coupon

A rusted lintel is a steel invoice and two hours. Cut-and-replace brick is units plus set time. Historic lime is mix time, not a bag. Color-match is a sample. The calculator prices the same wall three ways — smear, grind-and-point, rebuild — so you can see which method still keeps the margin when the owner asks you to “just match the other guy.”

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the tuckpointing bid calculator. It is not a structural specification, an engineered stamp, a historic-preservation determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge for tuckpointing?

Charge from wall area, method, access, and extras — not a published $8 / sq ft special. A ground-level Type N smear of a ranch veneer is a different job from a three-story historic lime grind with a swing stage, lintels, and cut-and-replace brick.

Does grinding change a tuckpointing bid?

Yes. A smear is a surface coat with no grind. Proper tuckpointing grinds the joint out, then points it. Rebuild is cut-out and relay. Matching a smear special on a grind-and-scaffold job is how a sold wall becomes a two-day loss after the first scaffold ticket.

How does access change a brick pointing price?

Ground is a ladder day. Two stories is scaffold rental and set hours. Three stories is a swing stage or mast climber. The access does not live in a published per-foot dump.

Is historic lime the same bid as Type N?

No. Type N is bags on a modern veneer. Lime putty is mix time and a different chemistry. Color-match is a sample invoice. The cheap special is almost always Type N on a one-story ranch.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Common questions

    Why does grind-and-point cost so much more than a smear on the exact same wall?

    Because a smear skips the grind step entirely — 0 grind hours and 0.055 point hours per sq ft — while grind-and-point adds 0.095 grind hours on top of 0.125 point hours, roughly four times the total labor per sq ft. Mortar follows the same jump, from $0.42 to $0.88 per sq ft, and grind-and-point is the only method that consumes grind blades at all. The method comparison prices the same wall all three ways so the gap shows up before you quote off a single per-square-foot number.

    Why does scaffold or swing-stage access cost so much even though it's not part of the wall itself?

    Because access is a flat setup cost tied to how the crew reaches the wall, not to how much wall there is. Ground access runs 0.7 hours and no equipment cost; scaffold runs 5.5 hours plus $480 of equipment; a swing stage or mast runs 9.2 hours plus $1,450. That charge is the same whether the wall being pointed is 20 sq ft or 200 — a small three-story job can carry more access cost than a large one-story job.

    Why does historic lime mortar cost more than Type N even on the identical method and wall?

    Type N portland comes premixed in bags and needs 0.4 hours of mix time with no per-square-foot premium. Historic lime putty needs 1.8 hours of mix time and carries a $1.35-per-sq-ft premium on top of the base mortar rate, because lime mortar is mixed and cured differently. Custom color-matched mortar goes further still — 2.6 mix hours, a $185 sample invoice, and a $2.15-per-sq-ft premium — all independent of which method (smear, grind, or rebuild) is doing the pointing.

    How is joint lineal footage worked out from the wall dimensions?

    From wall area times a joint density figure — length times height gives square footage, and that's multiplied by a lineal-feet-of-joint-per-square-foot rate to estimate how much joint the crew is actually working, not just how much wall face there is. That figure feeds the price-per-joint-foot number, which stays more consistent across walls of different proportions than price-per-square-foot alone.

    Do replacement bricks and lintels only add material cost?

    No — each replacement brick adds its own labor time on top of its own unit cost, and each lintel adds a much larger block of hours (1.8 hours per lintel) alongside its own material cost, because a lintel replacement is structural work, not a joint repair. Power-washing and control-joint caulk work the same way: each is a toggle or a quantity that adds its own hours and its own material line, contributing nothing when left off or at zero.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Tuckpointing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

“$8 a square foot, done” is not a price for a tuckpointing job — it is a price for one method, one access, and one mortar, quietly applied to every wall that gets called in.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a pointing job over the phone: multiply the wall area by a number and read it back. Homeowners and estimator sheets alike shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a ground-level veneer wall in ordinary condition, pointed with a surface smear and no grind, in plain Type N mortar — and then reused for every wall afterward, whether or not the next one needs a real grind, scaffold or a swing stage to reach, historic lime or color-matched mortar, or replacement brick and lintels.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the wall's length and height, the method (smear, grind-and-point, or cut out and relay), the access (ground, scaffold, or swing stage), the mortar (Type N, historic lime, or color-matched), replacement bricks, lintels, control-joint caulk, and your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, travel, and target margin. It prices the grind and point hours by method, the access hours and equipment by how the crew reaches the wall, and the mortar mix time and premium by chemistry, then returns the job price, the walk-away price, and the price per square foot — for this wall and this job, not a flat number for every wall.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate whether the joints get a surface smear or a real grind-and-point, even though a grind adds real hours per square foot the smear never needed. Prices grind hours and point hours separately by method preset, so a grind-and-point or a cut-out-and-relay job costs more than a point-only smear on the identical wall area.
Has no line for how the crew reaches the wall — a one-story ladder job and a three-story swing-stage job get the same square-foot rate. Prices access hours and equipment by preset: a ladder day, a scaffold set and rental, or a swing-stage rig and more set hours.
Quotes the same rate for plain Type N mortar and historic lime or color-matched mortar, with no line for mix time or the premium. Prices mortar mix hours and any color-match invoice or premium by chemistry, so historic or color-matched work is never quoted at Type N's rate.
Has no line for replacement brick, lintels, or control-joint caulk — a wall needing 80 bricks and 3 lintels gets the same number as one needing none. Prices replacement brick, lintels, and caulk by the piece or the foot, in both hardware and the crew hours to set them, as their own lines.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the price per square foot, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two walls, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own shipped starting examples:

A 320 sq ft single-story ranch veneer, pointed on the ground with a Type N smear and no grind, prices at $1,688.88 — $5.28 per square foot — on a job that costs $1,351.10 to run.

Take a 1,008 sq ft three-story historic wall instead — ground out and pointed with lime mortar from a swing stage, with 80 replacement bricks, 3 lintels, and 40 lf of control-joint caulk — and the job costs $17,720.03 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $22,150.03: $21.97 per square foot, about 4.2 times the smear job's rate, on roughly three times the wall area. Quoting the historic wall at the smear job's flat $5.28-per-square-foot rate prices it at $5,319.97 — $12,400.06 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $16,830.07 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin. Similar square footage on paper, one wall that pays and one that loses money the moment the grind, the swing stage, and the lime mortar show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a tuckpointing job wrong?

Because the cost driver is the method, the access, and the mortar, not the wall area. A 320 sq ft single-story ranch veneer, pointed on the ground with a Type N smear and no grind, is a short crew visit with basic mortar. A 1,008 sq ft three-story historic wall, ground out and pointed with color-matched lime mortar from a swing stage, with 80 replacement bricks and 3 lintels, needs a rigged lift, far more crew hours per square foot for the grind alone, historic mortar chemistry, and real hardware costs -- on a wall that is only about three times the area. A flat rate per square foot charges both the same because it was priced on the area, not the method, the access, or the mortar.

What does a flat rate per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Whether the joints get ground out at all, how the crew reaches the wall, and what the mortar actually is. A flat price has no line for a grind adding real hours per square foot beyond a surface smear, no line for a scaffold set or a swing-stage rig replacing a ladder day, no line for lime or color-matched mortar mix time and premium over ordinary Type N, and no separate line for replacement brick, lintels, or control-joint caulk. It also has no line for the extra crew hours all of that adds, since the flat number was set on wall area alone.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting examples: a 320 sq ft single-story ranch veneer, pointed on the ground with a Type N smear, prices at $1,688.88 -- $5.28 per square foot -- on a job that costs $1,351.10 to run. A 1,008 sq ft three-story historic wall, ground out and pointed with lime mortar from a swing stage, with 80 replacement bricks, 3 lintels, and 40 lf of caulk, costs $17,720.03 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices the job at $22,150.03 -- $21.97 per square foot, about 4.2 times the smear job's rate on roughly three times the area. Quoting the historic wall at the smear job's flat $5.28-per-square-foot rate prices it at $5,319.97 -- $12,400.06 below its own break-even cost, and $16,830.07 short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- a ground-level veneer wall in ordinary condition, pointed with a smear and no grind, in Type N mortar -- a flat per-square-foot number can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a grind-and-point job, a wall that needs scaffold or a swing stage, a historic or color-matched mortar, or a wall with replacement brick and lintels the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the method, the access, or the mortar until someone is on the wall, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or mortar costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your mason supply house's pricing, or your mortar costs. It takes the wall dimensions, the method, the access, the mortar, replacement brick, lintels, caulk, and your own wage, burden, overhead, travel, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this wall -- the arithmetic a flat rate per square foot skips, not a market survey.

Open the Tuckpointing Bid Calculator to price your own wall, or read how much to charge for tuckpointing.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, structural, or historic-preservation advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a structural assessment, a specification, or a finding that any wall is ready to point. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, mortar costs, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked examples.

This calculator vs. QuoteIQ

Two different shapes: QuoteIQ is a paid, ongoing CRM for running a masonry business's quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and photo-documented inspections across every job. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one wall cost, given its method, access, and mortar, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

QuoteIQ is a paid subscription CRM marketed to masonry and tuckpointing contractors alongside several other trades. Its publicly described feature set covers customer quoting, scheduling, invoicing, automated marketing and review requests, inspection forms that attach checklist photos to an estimate or invoice, and an AI estimator that drafts a starting line-item structure from a typed job description or a photo. It is sold as an ongoing account for the whole business, not a single-job tool. QuoteIQ's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or dollar figures, so none is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a paid CRM marketed in part to masonry contractors — are stated, and no dollar amount for QuoteIQ appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what QuoteIQ does. It does not market your services, hold a customer list, or keep an inspection record on a server. It takes one wall's length and height, a pointing method (smear, grind-and-point, or rebuild), an access method (ground, scaffold, or swing stage), a mortar (Type N, historic lime, or color-match), replacement brick, lintels, power wash, and control-joint caulk, and turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor, a three-method comparison on the same wall, and a printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most masonry contractors get different value from each: QuoteIQ (or a comparable CRM) for running quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and inspections across a business and every job it takes, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on what one wall should cost before a business system is involved. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off — which matters standing on a scaffold with no signal.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or QuoteIQ?

They fit different points in the job, and a masonry contractor of any size may end up using both. QuoteIQ is a paid subscription CRM marketed to masonry and tuckpointing contractors among other trades: customer quoting, scheduling, invoicing, automated marketing, inspection forms with photo evidence attached to an estimate, and an AI estimator that drafts a starting line-item structure from a job description or photo, run as an ongoing account across every job the business takes. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from wall length and height, method (smear, grind-and-point, or rebuild), access (ground, scaffold, or swing stage), mortar (Type N, historic lime, or color-match), replacement brick, lintels, power wash, and control-joint caulk, it turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A masonry business already running quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and photo-documented inspections across a full crew is better served by QuoteIQ or a comparable platform; a mason who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one wall should cost before opening a business system is in the right place here.

Does this calculator tell the difference between a smear and a grind-and-point job?

Yes, and that split is usually where a flat per-square-foot special goes wrong. A point-only smear over existing Type N bags is a surface coat with no grind; grind-and-point removes the old joint first, which is a different crew day; cut-out-and-relay is a third one again. This calculator prices each method's hours separately on the same wall, along with a three-method comparison, rather than quoting all three off one blended rate.
